Abstract

This study characterized the murine cervicovaginal microbiome (CVM) and its relationship to infection with Mus musculus papillomavirus 1 (MmuPV1) in immunocompetent FVB/N mice. Analysis of the natural CVM prior to intervention in two independent experiments revealed high inter-individual variability, with communities in Experiment 1 dominated by Pseudomonas and those in Experiment 2 dominated by Acinetobacter and Porphyromonas. Bray-Curtis dissimilarity confirmed these compositions were distinct (PERMANOVA P-value < 0.0001). Despite this variability, seven core genera were shared: Acinetobacter, Corynebacterium, Micrococcus, Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, and Streptomyces. MmuPV1 infection itself was found to shape the CVM, as infected mice exhibited altered microbial community composition compared to mock-infected controls. Furthermore, the viral inoculation dose influenced infection outcomes and associated microbial communities. Supervised analyses, including Partial Least Squares-Discriminant Analyses (PLS-DA) and Microbiome Multivariable Association with Linear Models version 2 (MAASLIN2), were used to predict microbial taxa associated with specific infection outcomes such as viral load and persistence. The evidence does not specify the exact identities of these predictive taxa or the direction of their associations. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the baseline murine CVM is variable but contains a core set of taxa, and that MmuPV1 infection dynamics are linked to specific shifts in cervicovaginal microbial communities.

Abstract

This prospective randomized controlled study evaluated the effectiveness of a structured oral care protocol in preventing oral mucositis in pediatric oncology patients undergoing chemotherapy. Thirty children aged 6 to 18 years with hematologic malignancies or solid tumors were randomized to an intervention group (n=15) or a control group receiving standard care (n=15). The intervention group received training and applied a monitored oral care protocol for 14 days. Oral mucositis was assessed using the Children’s International Mucositis Evaluation Scale (ChIMES) and the WHO Oral Mucositis Grading Scale on Days 0, 3, 7, and 14. Baseline characteristics were similar between groups. ChIMES scores were significantly lower in the intervention group compared to the control group by Day 14 (p=0.011). WHO scale scores also showed significant differences favoring the intervention group on Day 7 (p=0.002) and Day 14 (p=0.005). Within-group analysis indicated ChIMES scores in the intervention group significantly improved from Days 3 and 7 to Day 14. The evidence indicates that a structured, trained oral care protocol can reduce the severity of oral mucositis in pediatric patients receiving chemotherapy.

Abstract

This retrospective observational study evaluated the prognostic value of morphofunctional assessments for 12-month mortality in hospitalized patients receiving parenteral nutrition. The cohort comprised 614 adult patients (mean age 64 ± 14.6 years; 58.2% male). The one-year mortality rate was 26.1%, and the mean hospital stay was 27.9 ± 23.8 days. Survivors had significantly higher mean phase angle (4.9° vs 4.2°) and handgrip strength (19.4 kg vs 15 kg) than nonsurvivors. Receiver operating characteristic analysis determined sex-specific cutoff points for mortality prediction: phase angle thresholds were 4.2° for women and 4.7° for men, while handgrip strength cutoffs were 13.1 kg for women and 21 kg for men. Phase angle demonstrated superior predictive accuracy compared to handgrip strength. Twelve-month survival was 57% for patients with a low phase angle and 62.8% for those with low handgrip strength, versus 84% and 82.2% for patients with preserved values, respectively. In a multivariable logistic regression model adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index, each unit increase in phase angle and handgrip strength was associated with a reduced mortality odds ratio of 0.6 and 0.9, respectively. Malnutrition, identified in 63.9% of the cohort, and sarcopenia, present in 20.6%, were significantly more frequent among nonsurvivors. These findings indicate that low phase angle and low handgrip strength are strong, independent predictors of one-year mortality in this population.

Abstract
SMC4 expression is associated with poor prognosis and metastasis in prostate cancer. Analysis of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) data from 492 prostate cancer and 152 normal tissues showed no difference in SMC4 expression between groups, but patients with high SMC4 mRNA had significantly lower overall and disease-free survival (p < 0.01). In Oncomine datasets, SMC4 mRNA was elevated in metastatic versus primary tumors. In human prostate cancer cell lines (DU145, 22RV1) and a highly metastatic mouse cell line (RM1-LM), SMC4 was overexpressed. siRNA-mediated knockdown of SMC4 in DU145 and 22RV1 cells significantly inhibited proliferation, migration, and invasion (P < 0.01). Using CRISPR/Cas9 to knock down SMC4 in RM1-LM cells similarly diminished proliferation and migration in vitro. In a murine model, RM1-LM cells displayed higher lung metastasis capability than SMC4-knockdown cells. Transcriptomic profiling linked SMC4 knockdown to cell cycle and chromosomal separation pathways. Furthermore, SMC4 was found to interact with GLUT1, and its knockdown inhibited glycolytic rates in RM1-LM cells. These findings indicate that SMC4 promotes prostate cancer progression and metastasis, potentially through regulating glycolysis.

Abstract
SpecDB is a software platform for archiving raw nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) free induction decay (FID) data and associated experimental metadata within individual research groups. It is implemented as a local relational database using SQLite, managed by a Python software package. The platform addresses the challenge of inconsistent storage practices for FID data directories, which contain essential acquisition parameters, by providing a structured archive. The SpecDB schema is designed with two main components: one for describing the NMR sample through a hierarchical set of tables (PROJECT, TARGET, CONSTRUCT, EXPRESSION, PURIFICATION_BATCH, and Physical Sample Tube) and another for describing the FID data collection. The entire FID data directory is stored as a compressed binary large object. The schema is compatible with both the SPINE database and the NMR-STAR data dictionary used by the Biological Magnetic Resonance Data Bank (BMRB), enabling direct translation to NMR-STAR tags for deposition. Metadata describing the sample and experiment are entered using human-readable YAML (YAML Ain’t Markup Language) text files, which in the current implementation are created via user-edited Google Sheets. SpecDB includes a query system that allows structured queries against a defined Summary view, with results exportable as a directory hierarchy or as NMR-STAR files. The software is designed to be flexible to support future expansions of the schema for specific data pipelines.

Abstract
This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy of auricular therapy (AT) for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Following PRISMA guidelines, eight databases were searched from inception to December 22, 2024. Eighteen randomized controlled trials (RCTs) from mainland China, involving 1,231 patients, were included in the quantitative synthesis. The evidence was insufficient to support AT as a stand-alone intervention for PCOS. However, AT as an adjunct therapy showed beneficial effects on specific outcomes. When combined with a traditional Chinese medicine formula, AT reduced body mass index (BMI) (mean difference [MD]: –0.82, 95% CI: –1.60 to –0.03, P = 0.04) and scores on the Self-rating Anxiety Scale (MD: –3.81, 95% CI: –6.26 to –1.36, P = 0.002) and Self-rating Depression Scale (MD: –4.22, 95% CI: –7.74 to –0.69, P = 0.02), but not hormonal or other metabolic parameters. Adjunctive AT with metformin reduced BMI (MD: –0.77, 95% CI: –1.23 to –0.31, P = 0.0009), waist-hip ratio (MD: –0.03, 95% CI: –0.05 to –0.02, P < 0.0001), and luteinizing hormone levels (MD: –0.81, 95% CI: –1.05 to –0.57, P < 0.0001). Adjunctive AT with acupuncture reduced BMI (MD: –3.21, 95% CI: –5.09 to –1.33, P = 0.0008), luteinizing hormone, the LH/FSH ratio, and Homeostasis Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance. The protocol was registered with the Open Science Framework (DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/VBPSM).

Methods

Gastric cancer was induced in mice using the carcinogen N-Methyl-N-nitrosourea (MNU), administered in drinking water *ad libitum* at a concentration of 30 ppm on alternate weeks for a total exposure of 5 weeks, and mice were killed at 40 weeks (Fig. 1). The model utilized both C57BL/6 mice and p53 heterozygous knockout mice. Primary cultures were established from resulting gastric tumors, with fibroblasts removed during culture. Only one tumor from a male p53 heterozygous knockout mouse could be cultured long-term. Cells from this culture were subcutaneously transplanted into a C57BL/6 mouse, and the resulting tumor was excised and cultured again to establish cell lines. Through single-cell cloning, four distinct cell lines—YTN2, YTN3, YTN5, and YTN16—were subcloned and established (Fig. 1).

For *in vivo* characterization, 5 × 10⁶ cells of each line were implanted subcutaneously into C57BL/6 mice to assess tumorigenicity and spontaneous metastasis over 12 weeks (Table 1). Tumor growth was monitored, and metastatic rates to the lung, lymph nodes, and peritoneum were recorded. Histological analysis of original and transplanted tumors was performed using hematoxylin and eosin staining, and immunohistochemistry for pepsinogen 1 and class III mucin was conducted (Fig. 2). The p53 status of cell lines was assessed by PCR (Fig. 3F). *In vitro* growth rates of the cell lines were compared (Fig. 3E).

Microarray analysis was performed to compare mRNA expression between the more aggressive YTN16 subline and the less aggressive YTN2 subline (Table 2, Table S1). Based on a 121-fold higher expression of fibroblast growth factor receptor 4 (FGFR4) in YTN16 compared to YTN2, FGFR4 was selected for functional analysis. FGFR4 was knocked out in YTN16 cells using a CRISPR/Cas9 system, generating clones F7 and F87 with frameshift mutations (Fig. 6A,B). The *in vivo* tumorigenicity of these knockout clones was assessed. Furthermore, the FGFR4-selective inhibitor BLU9931 was administered at 30 mg/kg twice daily to treat mice with YTN16 subcutaneous tumors or peritoneal dissemination. The specific methods for inhibitor treatment duration or route of administration for dissemination models are not detailed in the provided evidence.

Methods

This retrospective cross-protocol, cross-sectional analysis compared immune responses and safety profiles across four randomized, controlled, double-blinded, multicenter trials: HVTN 100, 107, 120, and 702. The study population comprised HIV-uninfected adults who received a common vaccine regimen of ALVAC-HIV (vCP2438) at months 0, 1, 3, 6, and 12, plus a bivalent gp120 protein booster at months 3, 6, and 12, adjuvanted with either MF59, Alum, or AS01B. Immunogenicity assessments were performed on a per-protocol subset. The final analysis included 320 participants who received MF59, 27 who received Alum, and 46 who received AS01B (Table 1). Reactogenicity was assessed using a modified intent-to-treat population from all four trials, which included 3,000 participants receiving MF59, 36 receiving Alum, and 50 receiving AS01B. Demographic characteristics were similar across groups, with a median age of 24 years and 56.5% female participants.

Immunogenicity was evaluated at month 6.5. CD4+ T-cell responses were measured by intracellular cytokine staining (ICS) for IFN-γ and/or IL-2 expression in response to three antigens: 1086 gp120, TV1 gp120, and ZM96 gp120 (Table 2). IgG binding antibody (bAb) responses were assessed against multiple antigens, including C.1086C V1V2 Tags and Con 6 gp120/B. Reactogenicity and adverse event profiles were also compared.

Statistical comparisons of immune response magnitudes among positive responders were performed using Wilcoxon tests. Response rates were compared using Barnard's tests. A false discovery rate (FDR) p-value multiplicity adjustment was applied to all pairwise comparisons, as indicated by adjusted p-values reported in Table 2 and figures. The specific statistical tests used for comparing reactogenicity are not detailed in the provided evidence. All data visualizations, including comparisons of CD4+ T-cell magnitudes (Fig. 1), IgG bAb magnitudes (Fig. 2), and adverse events (Fig. 3), were generated from this analyzed dataset.

Methods

This retrospective observational study evaluated the first year of a regional Hub and Spoke model for pediatric type 1 diabetes (T1D) care implemented in July 2023 in Liguria, Italy. The model was coordinated by the Gaslini Institute (hub) and three peripheral pediatric departments (spokes). The study population comprised T1D patients aged less than 35 years in follow-up within this new system. Patients were categorized as transferred (previously followed at the hub), acquired (previously followed at a local center), or new onset. During the first two years of implementation, 129 patients were referred to the system. From this group, 88 patients (50 transferred, 38 acquired) who had available data at baseline and completed the 1-year follow-up were included in the final analysis; new-onset patients were excluded as no baseline comparison was possible. The flow of participant selection is detailed in **Figure 2**. Baseline characteristics of the included cohort (mean age 13 years ± 5.9, 53.4% male) are presented in **Table 1**.

The primary outcome was the change in glycemic control, measured as time in range (TIR) 70–180 mg/dL after 12 months of follow-up at a spoke center. Patients with insufficient continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data, defined as fewer than 12 days of valid recordings or <80% sensor usage in the assessment window, were excluded. Secondary outcomes included changes in other CGM metrics (e.g., time in tight range, time above/below range), adoption of technologies (real-time CGM and automated insulin delivery [AID] systems), clinical parameters (BMI), service utilization (number of outpatient visits), and environmental impact.

Data were collected at baseline (T0), corresponding to the first visit at a spoke, and at the 12-month (±3 months) follow-up visit (T1). All data were recorded in the REDCap® electronic platform. Technology use was categorized: glucose monitoring as self-monitoring of blood glucose, flash monitoring, or real-time CGM; insulin therapy as multiple daily injections, sensor-augmented pump, pumps with predictive low glucose suspend, or AID systems.

Environmental outcomes—travel distance saved, CO₂ emissions spared, and travel-related costs avoided—were estimated via travel analysis. The round-trip distance between each spoke and the hub was calculated using ViaMichelin® route planning. For each patient, the number of visits at the spoke during the follow-up year was multiplied by this distance. CO₂ emissions spared were calculated by multiplying kilometers saved by the national average emission factor for private vehicles in Italy (0.17 kgCO₂/km). Cost savings were estimated using the official per-kilometer operating cost (€0.367/km) for a reference vehicle (Fiat Panda 1.2 petrol). These annual estimates are shown in **Table 6**.

Methods

**Cell lines and culture**
The human osteosarcoma cell lines U2OS and SW1353, and the human osteoblastic cell line Saos2 were used. The specific culture conditions are not detailed in the provided evidence.

**Analysis of PRKCI expression**
The mRNA and protein expression levels of PRKCI in U2OS, Saos2, and SW1353 cells were evaluated using reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) and Western blot analysis, as shown in Fig. 1A-C. Protein levels were quantified relative to ACTB (β-actin).

**Plasmid and shRNA transfection**
For overexpression, SW1353 and U2OS cells were transfected with a PRKCI plasmid or an empty vector for 24 hours, with validation by RT-PCR and Western blot (Fig. 2A-D). For knockdown, cells were transfected with a PRKCI-specific shRNA (shPRKCI2) or a control shRNA (shcontrol) for 48 hours, as validated in Fig. 3A-D. The specific sequences and transfection reagents are not provided in the evidence.

**Functional assays**
Cell proliferation was assessed using the CCK-8 assay at multiple time points (Fig. 2E, F; Fig. 3E, F). Colony-forming capacity was measured by colony formation assay (Fig. 2G-J; Fig. 3G-J). Cell cycle distribution was analyzed by flow cytometry 48 hours after shRNA transfection (Fig. 4A-D). Cell migration and invasion were evaluated using Transwell migration and Matrigel invasion assays (Fig. 5), and a wound-healing assay (Fig. 6). For Transwell and wound-healing assays, cells were transfected with overexpression or knockdown constructs for 24 or 48 hours, respectively, as indicated in the figure captions for Fig. 5 and Fig. 6. All functional assays were performed in three independent experiments.

**Immunoprecipitation and pathway analysis**
The interaction between PRKCI and SQSTM1 was explored using immunoprecipitation, though the specific protocol is not detailed in the evidence. The effect of PRKCI knockdown on the Akt/mTOR signaling pathway was detected by Western blot analysis of total and phosphorylated levels of mTOR (Ser2448) and Akt (Ser473) in SW1353 and U2OS cells transfected for 48 hours (Fig. 8A-D).

**Clinical sample analysis**
Protein expression of PRKCI and SQSTM1 in osteosarcoma tissues, chondrosarcoma tissues, and adjacent nontumor tissues was assessed by immunohistochemistry (IHC), as represented in Fig. 7A-C. The correlation of PRKCI and SQSTM1 expression with clinical characteristics was analyzed, with data summarized in Table 3 and Table 4, respectively. The specific scoring criteria for IHC are not provided in the evidence.

**Statistical analysis**
Data are presented as the mean ± SEM from at least three independent experiments. Statistical significance is denoted as *p < 0.05 and **p < 0.01 in the figures. The specific statistical tests used are not detailed in the provided evidence.

Methods

We benchmarked 16 data integration methods on 13 distinct integration tasks, comprising two simulation tasks, five single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) tasks, and six single-cell ATAC sequencing (scATAC-seq) tasks (Fig. 1). These tasks represented challenges such as nested batch effects, integration across species and modalities, and scalability, drawing data from 23 publications and encompassing over 1.2 million cells (Table 1). Specific tasks included pancreas (16,382 cells; 9 batches), lung (32,472 cells; 16 donors), human immune (33,506 cells; 10 donors), human and mouse immune (97,952 cells; 23 samples), mouse brain RNA (978,734 cells; 4 datasets), and multiple mouse brain ATAC tasks with varying cell numbers and feature spaces (Table 1). Two simulation tasks (12,097 and 19,318 cells) provided ground truth for evaluation.

Each method was evaluated in up to 68 different setups per task, incorporating preprocessing decisions for scaling and highly variable gene (HVG) selection, resulting in 590 attempted integration runs. Methods that could not accept scaled input (LIGER, trVAE, scVI, scANVI) or required cell-type labels (scGen, scANVI) were run accordingly. Integration outputs (e.g., corrected matrices, embeddings) were evaluated separately, even from the same method.

Performance was assessed using 14 metrics across three categories: batch effect removal, conservation of biological variance from cell identity labels (label conservation), and conservation of biological variance beyond labels (label-free conservation) (Fig. 1). Batch removal metrics included kBET, k-nearest-neighbor graph connectivity, average silhouette width (ASW), graph iLISI, and PCA regression. Label conservation metrics included graph cLISI, Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), normalized mutual information (NMI), cell-type ASW, and isolated label scores. Label-free conservation metrics assessed cell-cycle variance, overlap of HVGs per batch, and trajectory conservation. New extensions to kBET and LISI scores were developed to handle diverse output formats consistently. An overall accuracy score was computed as a weighted mean of all applicable metrics, with a 40% weight for batch removal and a 60% weight for biological conservation. Usability and scalability were also evaluated, though specific measurement details are not provided in the evidence.

Methods

This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted to evaluate the efficacy of artificial intelligence (AI) tools for the three-dimensional segmentation of the upper airway using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) or CT scans. The review protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42024508004).

A comprehensive search of various databases and search engines was performed to identify all relevant English-language articles published up to April 25, 2025. The population of interest was studies assessing the upper airway. The intervention was the use of any AI tool, such as deep learning or machine learning, for image analysis. The comparator was manual analysis of CBCT or CT scans by a human. The primary outcome was the analysis of the upper airway on CBCT or CT images, with effect sizes including accuracy, precision, dice similarity score (DSC), total volume difference, intersection over union (IoU), recall, and other relevant segmentation parameters.

Study selection followed the PRISMA flow diagram (**Figure 1**). From an initial 113 records, 70 unique articles remained after duplicate removal. Abstract screening excluded 36 articles. Full-text review of 34 articles against eligibility criteria led to the exclusion of 23 studies for the following reasons: full-text unavailability, no use of AI, no use of CBCT/CT, upper airway not assessed, evaluation of skeletal malocclusions, lack of comparison with a human gold standard, or unclear results. Ultimately, 11 studies were included for qualitative synthesis, with 6 providing adequate data for meta-analysis (**Figure 1**).

The risk of bias for included studies was assessed, with most studies demonstrating a low risk of bias across most domains (**Table 1**). A summary of study characteristics, including data type, dataset sizes, AI tasks, hardware, and model structures, is provided in **Table 2**.

Meta-analysis was conducted for any parameter reported by more than one study with adequate information. This was possible for four effect sizes: precision, DSC, recall, and total volume difference. Weighted mean differences and 95% confidence intervals were calculated. All analyses were performed using STATA 17 software, with a significance level set at 0.05. Sensitivity analysis was performed using leave-one-out meta-analysis. Publication bias was estimated using Egger's regression test, with funnel plots evaluated where applicable. The specific results of these analyses for precision, DSC, total volume difference, and recall are shown in **Figures 2, 4, 6, and 8**, respectively, with corresponding sensitivity analyses in **Figures 3, 5, and 7**.

Results

A novel murine model of Achilles tendon transection and reattachment was established in forty-four 9-week-old male C57/BL6 mice to study tendon-to-bone healing, with assessments at 2 and 4 weeks postoperatively (Fig. 1). Histological evaluation revealed a disrupted native tissue structure that was replaced by a fibrovascular scar at the healing interface (Fig. 4B, C). While safranin O fast green staining indicated glycosaminoglycan deposition in the cartilage area, the original architecture was destroyed (Fig. 4E, F).

Micro-CT analysis of the calcaneus demonstrated a progressive healing process within the surgically created bone tunnel from 2 to 4 weeks postoperatively (Fig. 5B, C, E, F). Biomechanical testing showed that the failure force of the healing interface at 2 weeks constituted approximately 44.2% of that in intact tissues, increasing to 77.5% by 4 weeks (Table 2). The ultimate tensile strength also increased from the 2-week to the 4-week time point (Table 2). Specific statistical comparisons for stiffness and other biomechanical parameters are not provided in the evidence.

Gene expression analysis of the tendon-to-bone interface indicated that ACAN, SOX9, Collagen I (Col1a1), and MMPs were all overexpressed compared to the control group, maintaining high expression levels at both 2 and 4 weeks postoperatively (Fig. 7). The specific primer sequences for Col1a1 are listed in Table 1. The exact fold changes and p-values for individual genes beyond the general significance indicators in Fig. 7 are not detailed in the provided evidence.

Results

This exploratory study examined the oral microbiome in school-aged autistic (n=80) and non-autistic (n=40) children and the effects of a four-week intranasal oxytocin intervention in the autistic group. Participant characteristics are detailed in Table 1. At baseline, lower endogenous salivary oxytocin levels were associated with greater microbial evenness and diversity across all children (Fig. 2). Furthermore, twelve bacterial genera showed significant associations with oxytocin levels (Fig. 2).

In autistic children, four weeks of intranasal oxytocin administration (24 IU daily) was associated with specific changes in oral microbiome composition compared to placebo (Fig. 1, Fig. 3). Immediately post-treatment (T0-T1), oxytocin administration was associated with a significant increase in the abundance of *Centipeda* and a decrease in *Moraxella* (Fig. 3). At the four-week follow-up after treatment cessation (T1-T2), a subsequent reduction in *Rothia* was observed (Fig. 3). All results persisted after adjusting for nutrition and dental care (Table 2).

The genus *Moraxella* was of particular relevance. Its lower baseline abundance was associated with higher endogenous oxytocin levels (Fig. 2). Furthermore, within the oxytocin group, a stronger oxytocin-induced downregulation of *Moraxella* abundance from T0 to T1 correlated with greater increases in endogenous oxytocin levels (Fig. 4A). This downregulation was also associated with hypomethylation of the oxytocin receptor gene (OXTR) at CpG site -924 (Fig. 4B). The evidence does not specify the quantitative p-values or effect sizes for the microbial changes shown in Fig. 3, nor does it provide the specific correlation coefficients for the relationships shown in Fig. 4.

Results

A total of 80 eligible patients with refractory IBD were enrolled from three tertiary hospitals, comprising 52 with Crohn’s disease (CD) and 28 with ulcerative colitis (UC) (Table 3, Fig. 4). During the induction period, upadacitinib demonstrated substantial effectiveness. For CD patients, steroid-free clinical remission was achieved in 59.6% and clinical response in 61.5%, while endoscopic remission and response rates were 30.8% and 57.7%, respectively (Fig. 5A-D). For UC patients, the corresponding rates were 67.9% for steroid-free clinical remission, 71.4% for clinical response, 46.4% for endoscopic remission, and 60.7% for endoscopic response (Fig. 5A-D). These efficacy outcomes were sustained during the 12-month maintenance phase, with CD patients achieving 78.8% steroid-free clinical remission and 75.0% endoscopic remission, and UC patients achieving 85.7% and 78.6%, respectively (Fig. 5A, C).

Significant improvements in inflammatory and nutritional laboratory parameters were observed post-treatment. Trends showing reductions in fecal calprotectin (FC), C-reactive protein (CRP), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) levels are depicted in Fig. 6. Normalization rates for CRP and FC are shown in Fig. 5E-F. Trends for other laboratory outcomes, including white blood cell count (WBC), hemoglobin (Hb), platelet count (PLT), and lipid profiles, are presented in Fig. 7.

The safety profile was acceptable. The overall incidence of adverse events was 23.1% in CD patients and 14.3% in UC patients (Fig. 8). The most common adverse reaction was acne, occurring in 8.75% of all patients (Table 4). Discontinuation rates during the 12-month maintenance period were 7.1% for CD and 21.5% for UC (Fig. 8). Predictors of treatment response were analyzed using Lasso regression (Fig. 1) and the Boruta method (Fig. 2), with the performance of the resulting multivariate model shown by its receiver operating characteristic curve (Fig. 3, Table 2). Specific demographic and baseline characteristics of the cohort are detailed in Table 1 and Table 3.

Results

OSTF1 expression was elevated in human and experimental osteoarthritis (OA) cartilage. In cartilage tissues from OA patients (n=20), OSTF1 mRNA levels were significantly higher than in healthy volunteers (n=10) (Fig. 1A). This increase was confirmed at the protein level in a subset of samples (OA, n=4; healthy, n=2) (Fig. 1B). In a rat OA model induced by anterior cruciate ligament transection (ALCT), histological analysis confirmed progressive cartilage damage and proteoglycan loss at 2, 4, and 8 weeks post-surgery (Fig. 2A, B, C). Concomitantly, OSTF1 mRNA and protein expression were significantly increased in the knee cartilage of OA rats compared to sham-operated controls (Fig. 2D, E, F).

In primary rat chondrocytes identified by collagen II staining (Fig. 3A), an adenoviral vector delivering shRNA against OSTF1 (Ad-shOSTF1) was used for knockdown, with efficiency confirmed by qRT-PCR and western blotting (Fig. 3B, C, D, E). OSTF1 knockdown significantly alleviated IL-1β-induced chondrocyte injury. It increased cell viability (Fig. 4A), reduced TUNEL-positive apoptotic cells (Fig. 4B), and decreased levels of cleaved caspase-3 and cleaved PARP (Fig. 4C, D). Furthermore, OSTF1 silencing restrained IL-1β-induced inflammation, lowering mRNA levels of TNF-α and IL-6 (Fig. 4E, F). It also inhibited extracellular matrix degradation, as evidenced by increased mRNA and protein levels of collagen II and aggrecan, and decreased levels of MMP1 and MMP13 (Fig. 5A, B).

Transcriptomic analysis of IL-1β-stimulated chondrocytes with OSTF1 knockdown (IL-1β+Ad-shOSTF1, n=4 vs. IL-1β+Ad-shNC, n=4) identified differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (Fig. 6A, B, C). Pathway enrichment analysis indicated involvement of the NF-κB signaling pathway (Fig. 6D, E, F). Mechanistically, OSTF1 knockdown inhibited IL-1β-induced activation of the NF-κB pathway, reducing phosphorylation of NF-κB p65 (Ser 536) and its nuclear translocation (Fig. 7A, B). Bioinformatics analysis revealed that 18 DEGs from OSTF1-silenced cells overlapped with predicted NF-κB downstream targets (Fig. 8A, B), suggesting a coordinated gene network.

Results

We constructed a non-redundant benchmark dataset of antibody-antigen complexes for docking evaluation. The dataset was compiled from three complementary sources: the SACS and SAbDab resources, and an advanced search of the PDB. Complexes were only included if they were released after 1 June 2019, and structures containing only antibodies were excluded. To ensure a fair evaluation, we performed a de-redundancy procedure, retaining complexes only if they had corresponding unbound structures for both the antibody and antigen components. The final non-redundant dataset contains 105 antibody-antigen complexes with available unbound structures, prepared with aligned bound and unbound structure files (Fig. 1, Fig. 6). For 25 cases where unbound sequences were longer than bound sequences, we provided both truncated and untruncated structure files.

Compared to Docking Benchmark 5.5 (BM5.5), our dataset adds 112 total cases, comprising 14 single-domain antibody (sdAb) cases and 98 monoclonal antibody (mAb) cases, and increases the proportion of cases classified as Difficult (Table 1, Table 2). The dataset includes diverse antibody types such as human/humanized antibodies, sdAbs, and rodent antibodies. We classified the docking difficulty of all 112 cases into three categories—Rigid, Medium, and Difficult—based on interface RMSD (I-RMSD) and the fraction of non-native contacts (*f*<sub>non-nat</sub>), with specific criteria and case counts detailed in Table 3. Representative cases for each difficulty level are shown in Figure 2.

Further categorization of the complexes was performed based on the availability of unbound structures, resulting in four groups: unbound-unbound, unbound-bound, bound-unbound, and bound-bound (Fig. 3). The dataset also includes cases with notable structural features, such as complex 7A5S which contains two distinct antibody-antigen interfaces (Fig. 1), and complexes 6ZDG and 6ZER, which have 100% sequence identity but markedly different structures (Fig. 5). For some complexes, multiple unbound structures with different conformational changes were identified; for example, the antibody component of complex 6OTC has five unbound structures with Cα-RMSD values ranging from 0.784 Å to 2.254 Å (Fig. 8A). The complete benchmark dataset is available at https://github.com/Zhaonan99/Antibody-antigen-complex-structure-benchmark-dataset.

Results

The meta-analysis synthesized empirical evidence from studies published between 2004 and 2024 on the determinants of fast fashion consumption. A random-effects model was employed. The integrated research model, which extended the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) with brand-related constructs, is presented in Fig. 1.

The analysis revealed that brand attitude was the strongest predictor of purchase intention. Self-congruity with fashion brands was found to significantly enhance all TPB components, as evidenced by its positive relationships with attitude (Table 5), subjective norms (Table 6), and perceived behavioral control (Table 7). Perceived quality exerted a cross-cutting influence, positively affecting consumer attitude toward fast fashion brands (Table 8). The evidence also detailed relationships between perceived scarcity (PS) and the TPB constructs, showing its association with attitude (Table 1), subjective norm (Table 2), perceived behavioral control (Table 3), and intention to increase consumption (Table 4). The specific correlation coefficients (r) and sample sizes (n) for these relationships are detailed in the respective tables, but the exact numerical values are not provided in the available evidence. The findings indicate that perceived quality reinforces the multidimensional nature of consumer judgments, integrating both cognitive and social evaluations.

Abstract
The role of the transcriptional repressor REST in the adult brain remains incompletely understood. We generated a conditional mouse model (LSL-hREST) with a loxP-STOP-loxP-human REST (hREST) construct inserted at the Rosa26 locus. Crossing these mice with Nestin-Cre drivers to target neural stem cells resulted in heterozygous N-hREST embryos that were dead at birth and exhibited 30% smaller brains than control littermates. Immunofluorescence in these embryos showed exogenous hREST expression co-localized with the neural stem cell markers Nestin and SOX2, particularly around the ventricles. RNA sequencing of E18.5 N-hREST forebrains revealed a global transcriptional shift, with enriched pathways related to immune response compared to neuron-related pathways in controls. Quantitative PCR demonstrated an inverse relationship between hREST and Drd2 transcript levels. Chromatin immunoprecipitation in wild-type neurospheres confirmed REST binding to a specific site on the Drd2 promoter. In adult mice with REST overexpression in Drd2-expressing cells (D-hREST), this inverse relationship between hREST and Drd2 persisted at both the transcript and protein levels in the striatum. These D-hREST mice exhibited significantly decreased spontaneous locomotor activity in open-field assays, with a sample size of 5 mice per group for both males and females. Histological and TUNEL assays indicated no major structural abnormalities or apoptosis in the striatum of adult D-hREST mice.

Abstract
This prospective, randomized study compared the efficacy and safety of sliding cupping intervention versus narrowband ultraviolet B (NBUVB) phototherapy in patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. Sixty patients were randomized 1:1 to receive either sliding cupping, performed 30 times per lesion until the skin turned purple, or NBUVB, with initial doses of 300-800 mJ/cm² based on skin type, three times weekly for eight weeks. The primary endpoint was the mean percentage reduction in Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) score at week 8. Secondary endpoints included Physician’s Global Assessment (PGA), body surface area (BSA), pruritus visual analogue scale (VAS) scores, quality of life measures, and total response rate (≥30% PASI reduction). At week 8, the mean PASI reduction was 62.4% (95% CI, 54.9–69.8) in the sliding cupping group and 66.9% (95% CI, 59.6–74.2) in the NBUVB group, with no significant difference between them. The total response rates were 69.23% (18/26) and 79.17% (19/24), respectively, which also showed no significant difference (P = .526). Reductions in PASI, BSA, PGA, VAS, and quality of life scores were observed in both groups over time, but no statistically significant differences between treatments were found at any assessment point from baseline through week 12. Adverse event profiles were not detailed in the provided evidence. In conclusion, sliding cupping and NBUVB phototherapy resulted in comparable improvements in psoriasis severity and symptoms over an 8-week treatment course, with no significant difference in efficacy.

Abstract
This retrospective cohort study investigated the association between oral anticoagulation and clinical outcomes in hospitalized patients with liver cirrhosis and atrial fibrillation. The study included 502 patients at a single center from 2010 to 2019, with primary endpoints of new-onset portal hypertension and all-cause mortality. Propensity score matching was performed to mitigate selection bias, resulting in 283 matched patients for analysis. Among the total cohort, 240 new-onset portal hypertension events and 139 deaths were recorded. Logistic regression analysis before matching indicated that anticoagulation was associated with significantly reduced odds of new-onset portal hypertension (OR 0.310, 95% CI 0.152–0.592, P<.001). However, after propensity score matching, anticoagulation was not significantly associated with reduced mortality (OR 0.606, 95% CI 0.198–1.532, P=.328). Subgroup analyses suggested a potential protective effect of anticoagulation against mortality in women with a Child score of ≥3 (P=.013) and against new gastrointestinal bleeding events in specific patient subgroups (P<.05). The anticoagulated cohort was younger and had different baseline laboratory profiles compared to the non-anticoagulated group. These findings indicate that while anticoagulation may be linked to a lower incidence of portal hypertension, its association with reduced all-cause mortality in this matched cohort was not statistically significant.

Abstract
DNA polymerase theta (POLQ) is implicated in tumor progression, but its role in colorectal cancer (CRC) is not fully defined. Bioinformatics analysis of The Cancer Genome Atlas data revealed POLQ was overexpressed in 21 malignancies, including colon adenocarcinoma (COAD). In 48 paired clinical specimens, immunohistochemistry and western blotting confirmed POLQ was significantly upregulated in CRC tissues compared to para-carcinoma tissues (P<0.01 and P=0.01, respectively). High POLQ expression correlated with poor overall survival in these patients (P=0.033). Functional enrichment analysis of 251 POLQ co-expressed genes indicated involvement in cell cycle pathways. Experimentally, stable knockdown of POLQ in SW480 and HCT116 CRC cells significantly reduced proliferation, migration, and invasion. This was associated with decreased expression of MMP2 and MMP9 and inhibition of G1/M and S/M phase cell cycle proteins. Bioinformatic assessment of the tumor immune microenvironment linked high POLQ expression to altered infiltration of memory B cells, follicular helper T cells, and resting NK cells, and to differential expression of immune checkpoints including CD274. Drug sensitivity analysis suggested high POLQ expression was associated with lower IC50 for lapatinib and crizotinib but higher IC50 for roscovitine and salubrinal. These findings indicate POLQ promotes CRC aggressiveness and may influence the immune landscape and therapeutic response.

Abstract

A persistent challenge in proteomics is the analysis of small tissue samples with limited protein content. We developed a comprehensive seven-step workflow optimized for such samples, with emphasis on neuronal tissues like the trigeminal ganglion. Testing of lysis buffers revealed that a 5% SDS buffer enabled identification of 3662 proteins, outperforming a commercial miniprep kit (1283 proteins) and T-per with proteases (1995 proteins). Following protein digestion, tandem mass tag (TMT) labeling was employed to consolidate samples, with quality control confirming uniform labeling. For phosphoproteomics, a three-step enrichment strategy using Fe-NTA and TiO2 methods was implemented. This sequential process identified 1433, 199, and 62 unique phosphopeptides per step, respectively, culminating in the identification of 4454 total phosphopeptides and 2923 phosphoproteins (13,460 peptide groups). High-sensitivity LC-MS/MS analysis of trigeminal ganglion samples defined differential expression as a fold change >1.5 with a p-value <0.05. This analysis identified 61 upregulated and 33 downregulated peptides in the treated group's total proteome. The protocol provides detailed time considerations for each step, ranging from 1–2 to 6 hours. This workflow establishes a benchmark for precise and efficient proteomic and phosphoproteomic profiling of limited tissue samples.

Abstract

This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy and safety of teprotumumab versus placebo for thyroid eye disease (TED). A search of PubMed, EMBASE, and CENTRAL from inception to October 2025 identified seven eligible randomized controlled trials, comprising 438 total participants. All trials administered eight infusions of teprotumumab (10 mg/kg initial, then 20 mg/kg) every three weeks. Efficacy outcomes were pooled using random-effects models. Teprotumumab demonstrated significant benefits across all primary efficacy endpoints. The risk ratio (RR) for proptosis response (≥2 mm reduction) was 6.87 (95% CI, 3.32 to 14.24) and for overall response (composite of proptosis and Clinical Activity Score [CAS] reduction) was 7.82 (95% CI, 3.36 to 18.18). The mean reduction in proptosis was -2.46 mm (95% CI, -2.96 to -1.96). For diplopia response (≥1 grade reduction), the RR was 1.85 (95% CI, 1.28 to 2.68). The RR for achieving a CAS ≤1 was 3.39 (95% CI, 2.41 to 4.78), and the mean improvement in Graves’ ophthalmopathy–specific quality-of-life overall score was 10.87 (95% CI, 9.91 to 11.83). Safety analysis indicated elevated risks for hyperglycemia (RR, 2.82; 95% CI, 1.08 to 7.37), muscle spasms (RR, 3.83; 95% CI, 1.97 to 7.43), dry skin (RR, 6.54; 95% CI, 1.52 to 28.09), and hearing impairment (RR, 3.74; 95% CI, 1.26 to 11.13). In conclusion, teprotumumab is highly effective in improving proptosis, diplopia, CAS, and quality of life in TED patients but is associated with an increased risk of specific adverse events.

Methods

A melasma-like mouse model was established using 6-8-week-old female C57BL/6J mice subjected to a 28-day protocol combining broadband UVB irradiation, intramuscular progesterone, and emotional stress (Fig. 1A). Two modelling sites were used: the shaved head and the left ear. For the head group, UVB was delivered at 30 mJ/cm², while the left ear received 60 mJ/cm²; the right ear was shielded with tinfoil, and both eyes were protected (Fig. 1A). Progesterone was injected intramuscularly daily at two doses: a low-dose (P1: 0.4 mg/kg) and a high-dose (P2: 4 mg/kg), with injections alternated between hindlimbs (Fig. 1A). Emotional stress was induced using a rotating schedule of three restraint methods applied daily: 24-hour fasting or water deprivation (used twice weekly, never consecutively), confinement in a restraint device for 5 minutes, and tail-overhanging handstand for 2 minutes (Fig. 1A). This combined protocol was performed daily for 28 days, with photographs and observations recorded every 7 days.

Pigmentation changes in the modelling areas were assessed macroscopically and quantified by analyzing grayscale values from photographs using ImageJ software (Fig. 2A, B, C). For comparison, a separate UV-induced hyperpigmentation model was created using the same UVB dose but without progesterone or stress factors, with daily exposure for 28 days (Fig. 4A). In a therapeutic intervention, a subset of melasma-like mice received a daily oral gavage of tranexamic acid at 65 mg/kg for the 28-day modelling period (Fig. 6A).

Following the modelling period, mice were euthanized for tissue and serum collection (Fig. 1A). Skin tissues from modelled and control areas were processed for histopathological analysis using Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) and Masson-Fontana melanin staining (Fig. 3A, Fig. 5A). Melanin deposition was quantified by calculating the ratio of melanin granules to total epidermal and dermal area, epidermal area alone, and dermal area alone (Fig. 3B, C, D). Levels of tyrosinase (TYR), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and malondialdehyde (MDA) were assessed in skin and plasma, though the specific assays are not detailed in the provided evidence. Autophagy activity in lesional skin was evaluated via immunofluorescence staining for LC3 and p62 proteins, with relative fluorescence intensities quantified using ImageJ software (Fig. 8A, B, C, D). Specific sample sizes for each experimental group and the statistical tests used for comparisons (indicated by p-values in figures) are not provided in the evidence.

Methods

This study was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial involving 52 healthy adult volunteers (Abstract). Participants underwent a 2-week washout period before being randomized into two groups: 26 received probiotic chewing gum and 26 received control gum (Results). The probiotic gum contained *Heyndrickxia coagulans* SNZ1969® (Results). The intervention lasted 4 weeks, with participants instructed to chew one piece of gum daily (Abstract, Results). Dental plaque samples were collected at four time points: baseline after washout (T0), after two weeks of intervention (T1), after four weeks at the end of intervention (T2), and one week post-intervention (T3) (Abstract, Results, Figure 1). The primary outcome was characterization of the dental plaque microbial ecosystem, and the secondary outcome was qPCR-based detection of *H. coagulans* SNZ1969® in plaque from the intervention group (Results).

Of the 52 initial volunteers, 44 completed the study: 21 in the Intervention group and 23 in the Control group, resulting in a 13.5% dropout rate (Results, Figure 2). The mean age of all participants was 27.9 years, and 85.7% were female (Table 1). Compliance data indicated that 11 participants (7 Intervention, 4 Control) skipped some gum, with a mean of 1.0 ± 2.4 missed pieces out of 140 (range 0–12) (Table 1). Adverse effects, primarily gastrointestinal disorders, were reported by 17 participants (10 Intervention, 7 Control), but no statistically significant differences were found between groups for age, sex, compliance, or adverse effects (Table 1).

DNA was extracted from plaque samples. Quantitative PCR (qPCR) was used to detect and quantify *H. coagulans* SNZ1969®, with a limit of detection of 1.3 Log10 cell equivalents per ng of DNA (Results). The microbial community was assessed via 16S rRNA gene profiling to evaluate diversity and taxonomic composition (Abstract). Alpha-diversity metrics (Faith’s phylogenetic diversity, observed features, Pielou’s evenness, Shannon entropy) and beta-diversity (weighted/unweighted UniFrac, Jaccard, Bray–Curtis) were calculated (Figure 4, Figure 5). Statistical analyses included rank-based difference-in-differences models, Wilcoxon signed-rank and Mann-Whitney U tests for diversity metrics (Abstract, Table 3, Table 4), and differential abundance inference using a negative binomial modeling approach (Abstract, Table 6).

Methods

The Parkinson’s Disease Fluctuations treatment Pathway (PD-FPA) study was an Italian multicenter, observational study designed to describe the management of motor fluctuations in patients with advanced Parkinson’s disease (PD) (DOI:10.1080/07853890.2026.2628353). Ten centers enrolled consecutive patients between July 2018 and December 2020. Eligible patients were aged ≥18 years, had been diagnosed with PD 10-15 years before enrollment, and had experienced motor fluctuations for at least 2 years prior to enrollment.

Data collection included patient characteristics, PD stage, fluctuation details, and treatments. Information was collected retrospectively for approximately 1 year (Y1) and 2 years (Y2) before the study entry, and prospectively at enrollment (T0), 6 months (T1), and 12 months (T2) (Figure 1). The evidence does not specify the exact data collection instruments or procedures beyond the use of standard PD assessment scales.

The study enrolled 296 patients at T0 (60.1% male, mean age 68.0 ± 9.7 years) (Table 1). Clinical assessments included the Hoehn and Yahr stage, the motor examination (Part III) of the Movement Disorder Society Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS), the Non-Motor Symptom Scale (NMSS), and the Parkinson’s Disease Questionnaire (PDQ-39) (Table 1, Table 2). Motor complications were assessed using MDS-UPDRS Part IV (Table 3). Treatment data encompassed oral levodopa (daily dose and number of administrations) and all add-on medications (Table 1, Table 4, Figure 3). The use of advanced therapies, including infusion therapies and deep brain stimulation, was also recorded (Figure 4). Of the 296 enrolled patients, 227 completed the prospective follow-up to T2; 44 and 25 patients were lost to follow-up at T1 and T2, respectively (Figure 1). Statistical analysis methods are not detailed in the provided evidence.

Methods

**Clinical and bioinformatics analysis.** The correlation between SP4 expression and clinicopathologic features in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) was analyzed using the University of California Santa Cruz (UCSC) Xena online data (1). Survival analysis, including disease-specific survival (DSS) and progression-free interval, was performed using Kaplan–Meier analysis from the same source (Fig. 1D, E). The correlation between SP4 and PHF14 was analyzed using TCGA data (Fig. 4B). A cohort of 73 paired ESCC tissues and adjacent nontumor tissues was collected from patients, though the specific ethics approval and consent details are not provided in the evidence. The relevance between SP4 mRNA levels and patient clinicopathologic features for these 73 patients was recorded in Supplementary Table S1 (1).

**Cell culture and transfections.** The human ESCC cell lines EC109, TE-1, and SEG-1, and the normal human esophageal epithelial cell line Het-1A were used. Specific culture conditions are not detailed in the evidence. For functional assays, EC109 and TE-1 cells were transfected with SP4-specific siRNAs or an SP4 overexpression plasmid (Fig. 2I-L). Similarly, cells were transfected with PHF14-specific siRNAs or a PHF14 overexpression plasmid (Fig. 5). For rescue experiments, cells were co-transfected with SP4 siRNA-1 and a PHF14 overexpression plasmid (Fig. 6A-D). Pharmacological inhibition of Wnt signaling was achieved using LGK974 (Fig. 7A-E).

**Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) and Western blot.** SP4 and PHF14 mRNA expression levels in tissues and cell lines were analyzed by qRT-PCR, with GAPDH used as an internal reference (Fig. 1F, H; Fig. 4C; Fig. 5I, J). Protein expression was assessed by Western blot, also using GAPDH as a loading control (Fig. 1G, I; Fig. 2I-L; Fig. 3D; Fig. 4G, H; Fig. 5K, L; Fig. 6E, F; Fig. 7E, F). Each experiment was performed in triplicate (1).

**Functional assays in vitro.** Cell viability was measured by MTT assay (Fig. 2A, B; Fig. 5A, B; Fig. 6A; Fig. 7A). Cell proliferation was also monitored using a live-cell imaging system to count cell numbers (Fig. 2C, D; Fig. 5C, D; Fig. 6B; Fig. 7B). Cell-cycle distribution and apoptosis rates were analyzed by flow cytometry (Fig. 2E-H; Fig. 5E-H; Fig. 6C, D; Fig. 7C, D).

**Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) and luciferase reporter assays.** The binding of SP4 to the PHF14 promoter was predicted using the UCSC Genome Browser (Fig. 4A) and validated by ChIP-qRT-PCR (Fig. 4D). For luciferase assays, ESCC cells were transfected with a pGL3-PHF14-luc reporter plasmid containing the SP4 target sequences, and luciferase activity was measured 48 hours post-transfection, with Renilla luciferase as an internal control (Fig. 4E, F).

**In vivo xenograft experiments.** ESCC cells with stable SP4 knockdown were subcutaneously injected into nude mice to establish xenograft models. Tumor volume was monitored, and tumors were excised for analysis (Fig. 3E-G). Specific animal numbers and housing conditions are not provided in the evidence.

**Statistical analysis.** Quantitative data were analyzed by Student’s *t* test or Pearson χ² test as appropriate, as indicated in the figure legends (1). A *P* value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Methods

This study generated a comprehensive transcriptomic and spatial cell-type atlas of the adult mouse brain. The atlas was constructed by integrating two primary datasets: a single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) dataset and a spatial transcriptomic dataset generated using multiplexed error-robust fluorescence *in situ* hybridization (MERFISH).

The scRNA-seq dataset was generated from approximately 7 million profiled cells, of which approximately 4.0 million passed quality control (QC). This dataset combined cells from 10xv2 (n = 1,699,939 cells), 10xv3 (n = 2,341,350 cells), and 10x Multiome (n = 1,687 nuclei) platforms, as detailed in Fig. 1. The evidence does not specify the mouse strain, age, or detailed dissection protocols. Data processing involved separate initial QC and clustering for 10xv2 and 10xv3 datasets, followed by dataset combination, re-QC, and joint clustering. The 10x Multiome single-nucleus RNA-seq data was subsequently integrated to address gaps identified after joint clustering, as outlined in Extended Data Fig. 1a. Specific QC thresholds for gene counts and scores are shown in Extended Data Fig. 1b-c, but the exact numerical thresholds are not provided in the text.

The MERFISH spatial transcriptomic dataset comprised approximately 4.3 million cells. The workflow for MERFISH data generation and processing is summarized in Extended Data Fig. 2a. Data quality was assessed by correlating gene detection between MERFISH and bulk RNA-sequencing for four brain regions (Extended Data Fig. 2b) and by examining correlations between adjacent sections (Extended Data Fig. 2c). Distributions of cell volumes, gene detection, and mRNA molecule detection per section are shown in Extended Data Fig. 2d-f.

Cell-type classification was performed hierarchically, organizing cells into 4 nested levels: 34 classes, 338 subclasses, 1,201 supertypes, and 5,322 clusters, as summarized in the abstract. The transcriptomic taxonomy tree of 338 subclasses is presented in Fig. 1a. The correspondence between transcriptomic identity and spatial localization was analyzed by mapping cell types to anatomical regions in the Allen Common Coordinate Framework version 3 (CCFv3), with results visualized in a heat map in Fig. 6a.

All data are available through an online platform named the Allen Brain Cell Atlas, as stated in the abstract and results. Specific accession identifiers or repository URLs for the raw data are not provided in the evidence.

Methods

This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guidelines. No protocol was registered for this review.

A literature search was performed in PubMed, restricted to studies published in English within the last five years. The search utilized the keywords “GLP-1 agonists” and “weight loss,” which initially yielded 2085 studies. The screening process excluded 1885 studies that were not clinical trials or were in languages other than English. A further 104 trials were excluded by limiting the search to the last five years. The remaining 96 studies were assessed for eligibility, resulting in 21 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) being included in the final analysis (n = 7024 in pairwise analyses). The study selection process is detailed in a flowchart (Fig. 1), and the characteristics of the included studies are listed (Table 1).

The primary endpoint was the proportion of participants achieving any weight loss during follow-up. Data from 16 placebo-controlled trials were used for pairwise meta-analysis. The specific agents evaluated against placebo were semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, retatrutide, mazdutide, and cotadutide, with outcome data presented (Table 2). A fixed-effect model was used to calculate pooled odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Heterogeneity was quantified using the I² statistic. The evidence for this analysis is presented in a forest plot (Fig. 2).

A frequentist network meta-analysis was performed to compare the relative efficacy of different GLP-1-based pharmacotherapies, including both placebo and active comparators. Data for active-comparator trials are shown (Table 3). The results of the network meta-analysis were used to generate rankings based on the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA), presented in a ranking plot (Fig. 7). The risk of bias for all included RCTs was assessed, but the specific assessment tool used is not stated in the provided evidence; the results of this assessment are summarized (Table 4).
